title: Pay-Per-Attendance Social Prescriptions for Loneliness
one_liner: A settlement layer where health systems and employers pay small local groups (Men's Sheds, choirs, walking clubs) a fixed fee for every verified attendance by a doctor-referred lonely patient.
customer: Nonprofit-hospital community-benefit and population-health teams and self-insured employers first, then Medicare Advantage plans. The suppliers who get paid are local groups: Men's Sheds, choirs, run and walking clubs, craft circles.
problem: Social prescribing works abroad (Merton, London: GP visits down 33%, A&E visits down 50%) and WHO now attributes about 871k deaths a year to isolation. The US has no reimbursement path, so PCPs with 31-day waits have nowhere to send lonely patients. Third places run on volunteers and charity, and referral directories list them without paying them. Loneliness programs fail on retention, because people stop showing up after week 2.
solution: Screen for loneliness in primary care or at employer open enrollment (UCLA-3 or a similar short scale). The clinician sends an e-referral to a vetted local group, and the patient checks in by QR or NFC at each session. The buyer pays the group $8-15 per verified attendance, capped per member per month, and the platform keeps 15-20%. A dashboard tracks show rate at weeks 4 and 8, loneliness score change and ED or visit utilization. It is a payment and verification rail, not a social network. Groups are paid to be welcoming and to keep people coming, which is the opposite of an engagement-maximizing app.
why_now: WHO's June 2025 Commission report made loneliness a measured global health metric. Dating and social apps are stalling (Bumble layoffs, BFF relaunch), so friendship demand has no monetized supply. Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027 and lapsed ACA subsidies are squeezing hospital margins and pushing systems toward cheap prevention with measurable ROI. Employers are also cutting expensive drug benefits and looking for low-cost wellbeing spend.
revenue_model: Per-verified-attendance settlement (buyer pays, group gets about 80-85%), plus a small PMPM or annual platform fee for the outcome dashboard and clinic workflow. Later, Medicare Advantage supplemental-benefit contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not loneliness interventions. It is a business model for the hosts. A health payer already pays 10-100x $10 per avoided ED visit, and paying per attendance turns retention (the real failure point) into the unit of revenue. Referral directories like Findhelp route people but do not pay, and hosts cannot survive on referrals alone.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 small groups in one metro and sign each to a $10-per-attendance pilot. Sign one health-system community-benefit office or one self-insured employer for 100 referrals. Build check-in with a QR code and a spreadsheet-backed dashboard, no app needed. Measure week-4 show rate against the roughly 20-30% typical of unpaid programs, then use that number to pitch the second buyer.

title: Supply-Continuity Escrow for Hardware Startups
one_liner: Software-style source-code escrow, but for physical products: startups deposit CAD, BOMs and tooling data, and a pre-qualified micro-factory network is contractually obligated to keep making parts for buyers if the startup dies.
customer: Hardware startups selling to risk-averse institutional buyers (hospitals, cities, universities, fleet operators, utilities) who pay the fee, plus the buyers themselves as beneficiaries of an activation right.
problem: Procurement teams fear vendor death more than defects. A city buying 200 startup e-scooters or chargers, or a hospital buying a startup's carts or robots, has no continuity plan, so deals stall or die. When a hardware company collapses, its fleet is orphaned. The roughly 11,000 Fisker Ocean owners spent two years building their own parts supply chain through a nonprofit.
solution: A continuity package. Startups deposit CAD, drawings, BOM, supplier list, firmware build environment and key tooling data. We validate it by making trial 'trigger-ready' proof parts on printers, CNC and short-run PCB partners so that the plan is real and tested. A contract gives named buyers release rights on defined triggers (bankruptcy, 90 days with no shipments, end-of-life). Result: a one-page Continuity Letter the startup attaches to bids.
why_now: Hardware failures have piled up (Fisker, Canoo, Nikola and other consumer and mobility failures), so procurement officers have fresh horror stories. Low-cost printing, CNC and small-batch PCB fabrication now make it plausible to reproduce a wide range of parts locally without the original supply chain. Cities and health systems are buying more startup hardware in robotics, mobility and charging.
revenue_model: Annual escrow and validation fee from the vendor ($5k to $25k based on complexity), a paid proof-of-manufacturability audit, an activation fee (10% to 20% of fabricated-parts value) when triggered, and optional buyer-side monitoring of vendor health.
non_obvious_insight: It sells like insurance with a tiny loss ratio. The physical network is only activated a few percent of the time, but the deposit and the tested proof are what unlock enterprise deals for the startup. Because the startup pays to close a sale, the network is funded by growth spend rather than by rare disaster events. The hard part is proving manufacturability in advance, and that proof is the moat.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 hardware founders who are stuck in enterprise procurement and to 3 procurement or biomed managers who have been burned before. Offer a fixed-price $2,500 Continuity Letter (checklist audit plus one proof part) to the first five. Draft a simple template agreement with a startup-friendly law firm and line up two machine shops and a PCB house as network partners.

title: Supplier-Funded Books for Trade-Credit Customers
one_liner: Regional distributors pay to give each micro-customer done-for-you books, and get a permissioned live view of that customer's credit risk.
customer: Regional wholesale distributors (foodservice, produce, beauty supply, auto parts, building materials, uniform and linen) with 500-10,000 micro accounts on net-30 terms.
problem: Distributors extend trade credit to taquerias, salons and garages on gut feel, and bad debt and slow pay eat margin. Micro-customers keep no books, so there is no data to underwrite against. Ramp and Brex have moved upmarket and no vendor serves this tier. The owners will not pay for bookkeeping themselves.
solution: Every active account gets free, done-for-you books, funded by the distributor. Bank and card feeds are connected, the distributor's own invoices are auto-ingested, and receipts arrive by text or WhatsApp. The customer owns the ledger and can export it any time. With the customer's opt-in, the distributor sees cash coverage, the aging of the customer's other bills and payment-risk flags, and can raise limits or offer early-pay discounts to accounts that look healthy.
why_now: LLM categorization pushes cost per account below about $10 a month. The Fed's 2026 data shows microfirms are cash-tight (22% of applicants got no financing, and nonemployers lean on personal funds). The Bench collapse made data ownership and portability a selling point.
revenue_model: The distributor pays $10-25 per active account per month, justified by bad-debt reduction, shorter DSO and lower churn. Upsells: tax filing, payroll, and early-payment financing with a revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The micro-business will never pay for bookkeeping, but the party carrying its receivable will. A bad account costs a distributor thousands, while $15 a month is noise. Sponsorship also raises switching costs, so the distributor gets retention for free.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical in one metro, such as a produce or beauty-supply distributor. Get 12 months of invoices and payment history for 100 accounts, then backtest whether simple books-derived signals predict late payment. Sign a paid pilot covering 100 accounts, with success defined as DSO and write-offs.

title: Peak-Load Call Service for Mid-Size Factories
one_liner: Predict the handful of hours a year that set a facility's capacity charge and alert the plant manager to cut load, paid as a share of verified savings.
customer: Commercial and industrial sites of 300 kW to 5 MW in PJM (and ERCOT 4CP) territories that demand-response aggregators ignore: cold storage, water and wastewater plants, plastics and aggregates producers, ice rinks and indoor farms. Energy brokers and consultants are the channel.
problem: A customer's capacity tag (PLC) is set by usage during a few system-peak hours, and its cost then sits on every bill for a year. PJM capacity prices have risen roughly tenfold since 2024/25, with recent auctions clearing at the cap of about $330/MW-day, so a 1 MW site's tag is worth six figures. Owners either never curtail and overpay, or curtail on 20+ hot days and lose production. Aggregators skim 20 to 40% and focus on large accounts.
solution: Model the probability that each upcoming hour ranks in the system's top peaks for the site's zone or utility rules. Use weather ensembles, load forecasts, calendar effects and, critically, the season's running maximum so far. Send a text or BMS signal with the expected value of curtailing against the plant's own curtailment cost. Cut curtailment days from about 25 to about 8 and stop alerting once the peaks have been 'caught'.
why_now: Data-center load growth has pushed PJM capacity clearing prices to the cap two auctions in a row, and those costs are now hitting commercial bills. Open AI weather ensembles (ECMWF AIFS, NOAA) make sharper probabilistic forecasts cheap. The just-finished 2026 summer is fresh evidence for a backtest pitch.
revenue_model: 20 to 25% of verified savings (measured from the next year's PLC change), a $250 to $500 monthly alert subscription, and $2K to $5K paid load audits. Brokers and consultants get a channel rebate.
non_obvious_insight: Quants see 'top 5 hours out of 4,000' as an order-statistics and optimal-stopping problem with asymmetric payoffs, not a pure forecasting problem. As the season's record load rises, the threshold to enter the top 5 becomes known, the option value of alerts collapses, and you can stop curtailing early. Incumbents earn more the more events they call, so their models over-alert. The savings show up a year later on an invoice nobody links to behavior, so customers underinvest without a counterfactual 'what your tag would have been' report.
first_30_days: Use the off-season to pull public PJM hourly load and zonal data, backtest 2019 to 2026 peaks, and generate a free 'what your tag would have been' report for 100 facilities found through EIA and utility-tariff lists. Sell $3K load audits to the first five, sign shared-savings pilots for summer 2027, and recruit two energy brokers as channel partners.

title: Robot Access Passport for Commercial Buildings
one_liner: One certified robot identity, insurance certificate and elevator/door gateway that lets any delivery, cleaning or humanoid robot enter a building, with landlords collecting a fee.
customer: Owners and managers of office towers, multifamily REITs, hospitals, hotels and malls, who pay a subscription. Robot operators pay per-robot access fees.
problem: Every robot vendor negotiates separately with building management on elevator integration, insurance, liability and hours. Buildings have no policy or tooling, and incidents have no clear owner. This gets worse as sidewalk, cleaning, security and humanoid pilots multiply.
solution: A $1-2k building-side controller integrated with elevators, doors and turnstiles through existing vendor APIs or relays, plus a registry that verifies operator, insurance, firmware version and incident hotline. A policy engine sets quiet hours, zones and speed limits, with usage-based billing. Landlords earn a share of access fees, and robot operators integrate once for many buildings.
why_now: About 22k humanoids shipped in H1 2026, delivery robots and drones are moving to multifamily, and regulators (NHTSA's July 2026 first-responder letter) are pushing for accountability. Buildings are the next permission bottleneck.
revenue_model: $150-400 a month per building in SaaS plus $5-15 per robot per month in access fees, split with the landlord, and installation margin.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource in robot deployment is permission, and building owners are the gatekeepers with zero tooling. A neutral gatekeeper standard is a two-sided network, like 'ID.me plus a certificate of insurance for robots', and landlords get paid to adopt it.
first_30_days: Approach 2 property managers in one metro where delivery robots already operate. Build an integration for one elevator vendor's open API, get a certificate-of-insurance template from a broker, and charge $500 a month for the pilot.

title: Chargeback Guarantee for Agent-Placed Orders
one_liner: A merchant-side gateway that checks the shopper's signed mandate against the cart, keeps a tamper-proof decision record, and reimburses chargebacks on approved agent orders.
customer: Shopify, BigCommerce and headless merchants doing $5M-$100M GMV that have switched on agentic checkout (ACP, UCP, AP2) and whose acquirers watch their dispute ratios.
problem: Fraud engines score human signals (device, mouse, session) that agents lack, so agent orders are either falsely declined or approved blind. Disputes have no rulebook: neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding chargeback rule for agent-initiated purchases, the record shows only merchant, timestamp and amount, and Visa's dispute threshold tightened from 2.2% to 1.5% on 2026-04-01. Merchants also have to support ACP, UCP, AP2, MPP and x402 separately.
solution: One integration that accepts all five protocols. It cryptographically verifies the user-signed mandate (spend cap, item constraints, expiry, agent identity) against what was actually ordered, stores an immutable decision record, and auto-builds representment packets. Orders that pass are guaranteed: we pay the chargeback and the fee. Underwriting rests on mandate-versus-cart match, not on behavioral fingerprinting.
why_now: The protocols went live in the last 8 months (MPP 2026-03-18, plus ACP, UCP, AP2, TAP, Verifiable Intent). Agent usage is about 62% at comparison but only about 23% at checkout, so trust is the bottleneck. The Ninth Circuit's 2026-08-04 Comet ruling treats the agent as the user, and there is still no fault rulebook from the networks.
revenue_model: 0.5-1.0% of guaranteed agent-order GMV plus $299-1,999 per month gateway SaaS. The guarantee reserve is backed by a $1-2M capital line or a quota-share reinsurer. Loss data can later be licensed to insurers and networks.
non_obvious_insight: Incumbent fraud models are trained on human behavior, so agent traffic is behaviorally blank. The right signal is the mandate, not the session. Whoever holds the mandate-versus-cart record and the loss outcomes becomes the arbiter that networks, acquirers and insurers will need, and that same data is the missing underwriting telemetry for agent risk generally. Merchants will not want to pick among five protocols, so the guarantee is the wedge for owning the plumbing.
first_30_days: Ship a Shopify app in shadow mode for 15-20 merchants: tag agent-origin orders (agent referrers, ACP/UCP headers), log mandates, and back-test which orders would have been disputed. Offer the first 5 merchants a 90-day guarantee capped at $50k each, funded by founder capital plus a small MGA or reinsurer line, at about 0.75% of agent GMV. Publish the observed dispute rates as the pricing basis.

title: Scam-Baiting AI Fleet Selling Mule Intel
one_liner: Thousands of realistic AI victims answer scammers' calls and chats around the clock, extract the accounts and wallets they are told to pay, and hand them to the holding institutions before real victims do.
customer: Banks, neobanks, BaaS sponsor banks, stablecoin issuers, exchanges and payment apps. Telcos are a secondary buyer.
problem: Scam cash-out depends on mule accounts and wallets, but institutions learn about them only after victims pay. Scam revenue reached about $17B in 2025, and AI-enabled operations earn far more per operation, while defense stays manual and reactive.
solution: Persona-driven voice and messaging agents on real-time speech-to-speech models answer phone numbers seeded onto scam lead lists and respond to smishing and wrong-number openers. They keep scammers engaged (burning their labor), record payment instructions, and extract payee accounts, wallets and gift-card destinations. Evidence-graded indicators go via API to the institution that holds the account so it can freeze and close before a real victim pays.
why_now: Real-time speech models made convincing multi-turn calls cheap in 2025-26. Stablecoin issuers and cross-industry units now freeze funds quickly, and the US-UK scam-center coordination raises appetite for actionable intelligence.
revenue_model: $200-1,000 per confirmed account or wallet plus $5-20K per month subscriptions, and data licensing to fraud vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Scammers' scarce resource is human operator time, so AI victims raise their cost per victim while producing intelligence with zero victim cost. Institutions pay far more for pre-loss intelligence than for post-loss forensics.
first_30_days: Build 20 personas across phone and WhatsApp. Run them against inbound spam numbers and produce about 100 verified indicators. Sell 2 neobanks and 1 exchange a $10K paid pilot, with counsel reviewing recording-consent rules first.

title: AI-Off Proficiency Checks for Clinicians
one_liner: E.M. Forster's The Machine Stops and Asimov's The Feeling of Power turned into recurrent, pilot-style checks that measure whether clinicians still perform well when the AI is switched off.
customer: GI and radiology group practices, hospital medical staff offices (ongoing professional practice evaluation and credentialing), physician-owned malpractice carriers seeking premium-credit evidence, and residency programs.
problem: Routine AI assistance may erode unaided skill. A 2025 Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology study of 19 experienced endoscopists in Poland found adenoma detection in non-AI colonoscopies fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after AI exposure (the study is observational and has been contested). No one measures unaided proficiency, unlike pilots' manual-flying currency, and outages or out-of-distribution cases will expose the gap.
solution: A quarterly, 25-minute, blinded and timed case set (videos and images with expert ground truth) delivered with AI overlays disabled. Scores are benchmarked against each clinician's own baseline and peer cohort, with drift alerts, targeted micro-drills, and a certificate for credentialing files and insurers. Add an AI-outage drill for departments (tabletop plus live). Start with colonoscopy, then extend to mammography and other AI-assisted reads.
why_now: AI computer-aided detection is now routine in colonoscopy and mammography. The deskilling study made the risk concrete and quotable. Malpractice carriers and hospital counsel are looking for defensible evidence, and the Joint Commission already requires ongoing professional practice evaluation.
revenue_model: $600-1,500 per clinician per year, carrier-funded programs paid per insured group, and enterprise licenses for health systems.
non_obvious_insight: Sell it as insurance evidence and credentialing paperwork, not education. Aviation shows regulators and insurers accept currency requirements once a failure mode is measured. The pre- and post-adoption unaided performance record is also what a hospital will need to defend an AI-related malpractice case, so buyers are motivated to start their baseline now.
first_30_days: License public polyp-video datasets and recruit two GI academic advisors to write ground truth. Build 10 case sets and pilot free for eight weeks with two GI groups. Pitch one physician-owned malpractice carrier on a premium credit for participating groups, then charge about $900 per clinician per year.

title: Verbal-Promise Ledger for Mine Community Relations
one_liner: A voice-first, offline-capable phone tool that turns every promise a mine makes at community assemblies (Spanish, Quechua, Aymara) into a tracked commitment register the community can verify by WhatsApp.
customer: Heads of social performance and community relations at mid-tier copper and lithium operators and developers in Peru, Chile, Argentina and Bolivia. The second buyer is the E&S team at the lender or DFI (IFC, EXIM, DFC, export credit agencies). Budget is roughly $2-6k per month per project, charged to a risk or permitting line, not to IT.
problem: Insiders know that projects get blockaded over small, forgotten verbal promises, not over the headline issue. Examples are a promised well repair, a local-hire quota, or a dust-suppression schedule. The promise is made at a 2pm assembly and recorded on a paper acta, in a notebook, or in a WhatsApp voice note. Community-relations staff rotate every 12-24 months, contractors make their own promises, and nobody indexes the actas. Two years later the community says 'you promised' and shuts the road. The Las Bambas corridor closures, Jujuy lithium protests and Tia Maria all fit this pattern of trust debt. The mine cannot prove what it did or did not commit to, and neither can the community.
solution: Field officers record assemblies on a phone and snap a photo of the signed acta. Speech-to-text, tuned for Andean Spanish and human-checked for Quechua and Aymara, extracts discrete commitments: who promised what, to whom, and by when. Each one is assigned an internal owner and a due date. Community leaders get a receipt as a WhatsApp voice note or pictogram and can confirm, dispute, or mark it done. Ops managers and the CFO see 'commitment debt' aging, like a technical-debt dashboard. One-click exports meet IFC Performance Standard 1 and Equator Principles grievance and commitment register requirements. Community-side verification is the moat. It makes this a trust tool, not a surveillance tool.
why_now: Speech models are good enough for accented, code-switched Spanish, and usable for Quechua with a human in the loop. WhatsApp is universal in rural Andean communities. Lenders are demanding auditable social-license evidence for critical-mineral financings, including EU CRMA strategic projects and US DOE/DFC/EXIM deals. Argentina's RIGI regime is pulling lithium and copper projects into provinces with little consultation history. Peru and Chile have changed governments (2026), which reopens community negotiations. Staff turnover after the 2024-25 cost-cutting rounds has made institutional memory worse.
revenue_model: SaaS at $2-6k per month per project, plus a per-community onboarding fee ($1-3k). A one-off 'commitment debt audit' of historical actas is priced at $5-15k. Later, a lender-grade verified engagement score and a lender or insurer data licence.
non_obvious_insight: Conflict risk is mostly commitment debt, meaning unanswered small promises lost through staff rotation, not big ideological opposition. Buyers think they need sentiment analysis. What they need is a receipt system. Giving the community the receipt is what makes the mine's data credible to lenders and inspectors.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, recruit two junior or mid-tier developers currently in a consultation round. Sell a $5-10k 'commitment debt audit': scan their last 12 months of actas and meeting minutes, and use an LLM plus a local linguist to extract every commitment and flag the overdue ones. This works with no integration, just PDFs and photos. The overdue list is usually shocking, and it converts to a SaaS pilot for the next assembly round. Use a WhatsApp Business API bot and an offline recorder app for v1. Do not build a custom platform yet.

title: SOX Evidence Packs for Agent-Run Controls
one_liner: Control libraries, walkthrough scripts and test evidence that let auditors accept AI agents inside financial close, AP and reconciliations.
customer: Controllers, SOX program managers and internal audit at US public companies ($500M-$10B revenue) piloting agents in finance, plus mid-tier audit firms that must test them.
problem: As of mid-2026 the PCAOB has no AI-specific standard. Auditors ask how agent actions are authorized, logged and reviewed, and whether agent-generated walkthroughs count as sufficient evidence. FEI's Committee on Corporate Reporting published an AI-in-ICFR framework in June 2026, but finance teams have no packaged controls or evidence format.
solution: A library of agent-specific controls mapped to COSO 2013 (access, prompt and model change management, completeness, override monitoring), with test scripts, sampling templates and an evidence collector that exports action logs, approval trails and change tickets in auditor-ready format. Start with a pre-interim readiness assessment.
why_now: Calendar-2026 audits are entering interim testing, the June 2026 FEI framework gives a hook, and a standards vacuum means the first accepted evidence format wins.
revenue_model: $20-$60k readiness assessments, $3-$8k/month evidence subscriptions, and license deals with audit firms.
non_obvious_insight: In a standards vacuum, the first packaged evidence format an audit firm accepts becomes the de facto standard, as SOC 2 report formats did for cloud. Auditors are also under pressure to have an answer.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 former Big-4 SOX auditors and write 25 agent controls. Run free readiness workshops for 10 controllers already piloting agents in AP or close, and convert 2-3 to paid assessments.

title: Cure Desk: Medical-Bill Triage for Delinquent Tenants
one_liner: A landlord-paid service that turns a late-rent notice into a medical-bill rescue, using hospital charity care, bill negotiation and coverage re-enrollment to free up the cash that pays the rent.
customer: Multifamily and single-family-rental operators (500-20,000 units) pay per cured account.
problem: 20% of renter households paid late or missed rent in 2025, and middle-income households jumped from 14.3% to 21.6%. About 4.8M people lost coverage after enhanced ACA subsidies expired. Landlords now face AI-assisted pro se tenant filings (41,000+ federal pro se cases in 2025) and increasingly conclude that cash-for-keys is cheaper than winning an eviction.
solution: When a resident is 3-5 days late, the property manager sends an opt-in text. If medical bills or a coverage loss are the cause, an advocate applies to the hospital's financial-assistance program (nonprofit hospitals must have one), negotiates the bill, sets payment plans and opens a special enrollment period. The landlord pays a success fee (roughly $300-500) only when arrears are cured, versus thousands per eviction.
why_now: Subsidy expiry created millions of self-pay patients in 2026, delinquency is at series highs, and the legal cost of eviction is rising with AI-generated filings. Medicaid churn from Jan 2027 will add more.
revenue_model: Success fee per cured account, with an optional $/unit/month retainer for early-warning outreach.
non_obvious_insight: A missed rent payment is the earliest and most reliable distress signal in consumer finance, and it lands on the one party with the data, scale and cash motive to pay someone to fix it. A tenant's hospital bill is far more negotiable than a landlord's arrears, so the fix comes from the health side.
first_30_days: Recruit two ex-hospital financial counselors. Sign two mid-size operators and run 200 delinquent accounts manually via SMS and a shared inbox. Track cure rate and cost per cure. Landlords pay only after cure.

title: Idle-Still Co-Packing for Zero-Proof Brands
one_liner: Turn distilleries' idle stills and bottling lines into contract capacity for dealcoholized and botanical spirit brands.
customer: Craft and mid-size distilleries with underused capacity, and zero-proof beverage brands that need production.
problem: US spirits sales fell 15.4% and Diageo's US tequila fell 23% as GLP-1 use spreads, leaving distilleries with fixed costs and empty lines.
solution: A capacity broker and operations layer that matches idle distilleries to zero-proof and functional-tonic brands, handles TTB and formulation paperwork, and standardizes QA and scheduling.
why_now: GLP-1 adoption is now visibly cutting alcohol volumes, and the non-alcoholic segment is growing but short of contract capacity with spirit-grade distillation.
revenue_model: 10-15% take on co-pack contracts plus fees for compliance and formulation services.
non_obvious_insight: The first casualties of GLP-1 in beverages are asset-heavy distillers, whose stills are worth more as co-packers to the segment that is replacing them. Grain and agave growers downstream are the next to feel it.
first_30_days: Interview 20 distilleries about idle capacity, line up 5 zero-proof brands with pending production needs, and run one paid pilot batch with a partner distillery.

title: Per-Class Portable Benefits for Fitness Instructors
one_liner: A payout layer that skims a small per-class contribution from studios and class apps into each 1099 instructor's own injury income protection, health-premium credit and retirement account, structured to give studios legal cover under portable-benefits laws.
customer: Boutique studio groups with 5-30 locations, gym franchisees, class marketplaces and corporate-wellness providers that use 1099 instructors, paying $0.50-2 per class. Instructors opt in for bonus benefits. Trainer associations are a distribution channel.
problem: Several hundred thousand US fitness instructors and trainers work at 3-6 venues, mostly as part-time or self-employed workers with no disability cover, workers' comp or retirement plan. Enhanced ACA subsidies expired in 2026, federal-marketplace enrollment fell about 21%, and an estimated 4.8M people became uninsured, so self-employed instructors' premiums jumped. Injuries to voices, knees and backs end income immediately. Studios face misclassification suits, and because each studio has separate payroll, no one accumulates benefits.
solution: Integrate with scheduling systems (Mindbody, Momence, Walla) to read classes taught. Studios contribute a per-class amount into each instructor's benefits wallet, for example $1.25. The wallet buys short-term income protection through a partner insurer, an ACA premium top-up or HSA deposit, and an IRA contribution. Contributions follow the instructor across venues. The structure is designed to fit safe harbors in states that have passed portable-benefits laws since 2023 (verify current list and get legal review).
why_now: ACA subsidy expiry hit self-employed workers in 2026. A handful of states have passed portable-benefits laws since 2023 that shield platforms from treating contributions as employment evidence. Class-pass economics keep instructors spread across venues. Misclassification exposure keeps studio owners nervous.
revenue_model: A platform fee of 8-10% of contributions, insurer commissions of 12-20% on income protection, and interchange on a benefits card. 10,000 instructors at $2,000 a year in contributions is $20M of flow and about $1.6-2M of revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Portable benefits have struggled with gig platforms because work units are messy. Fitness instructors' work is already itemized in software as class events, so a contribution per class is a natural unit. Fitness is the ideal beachhead because work is high-frequency, discrete, multi-venue and tracked, and instructors are health-literate and physically at risk, so they will value injury protection.
first_30_days: Sign one 10-studio group. Run contributions through a simple ACH from the studio. Partner with an existing accident and disability MGA for a $2-4 a week income-protection policy. Enroll 100 instructors and pilot a $1-per-class contribution. Track instructor retention at the studio and first claims. Target 500 instructors within six months.

title: Second-Look Verification for Imagery-Based Nonrenewals
one_liner: A $50-80, 48-hour human check between an aerial-imagery flag and a nonrenewal, sold to carriers' compliance teams.
customer: Regional and mid-size homeowners carriers and MGAs in California, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and New York, bought by underwriting and compliance leads.
problem: Imagery-driven nonrenewals are generating regulatory heat (a Florida owner with 52 claim-free years was dropped with no inspection). California AB 75 became operative July 1 2026, requiring notice, a copy of the photos, a dispute path and a remediation window. CT, NH and PA regulators say imagery alone is insufficient, and a NY bill is pending. In-person inspections cost far more and take weeks.
solution: A guided homeowner video capture with fraud checks, or a local gig inspector, returning structured findings mapped to the carrier's rules. It auto-generates the compliant notice package and remediation checklist, and keeps an audit log for regulators.
why_now: AB 75 took effect July 1 2026, and other states are moving.
revenue_model: Per flagged policy plus a platform fee.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators demand more than imagery, but nobody wants $250 inspections. The lower price point makes compliance affordable at scale and sells to a budget-holding compliance team.
first_30_days: Call 10 regional carriers' compliance heads and pilot with 200 flagged policies. Prove the share of imagery flags that human review clears.

title: Micro-Bounties for Humans to Rescue Stuck Robots
one_liner: An on-demand app where robots and AVs post 30-second physical tasks (close a door, plug in a charger, move a cone, lift a robot over a curb) and nearby humans get paid instantly.
customer: Operators of sidewalk delivery robots, robotaxi and AV fleets, drone hubs, cleaning robots and warehouse AMRs, paying about $3-15 per task.
problem: Autonomy fails at the last physical one percent. Only 54% of Waymo's first 86M miles carried a passenger and each reset cycle takes about 2 hours. Dispatching a staffer or tow costs far more than the fix, and each fleet builds its own field-ops team.
solution: An SDK in which the robot emits a help request with location, photos and a vision-language-model task description. Nearby vetted people accept it, the robot's own sensors verify completion, and payout is instant. Strict safety rules prevent anyone touching moving machines. Start with door-ajar, debris and stuck-at-curb tasks.
why_now: Robot fleets are scaling faster than field crews (Waymo about 500k rides a week, sidewalk fleets in the thousands), and AV firms have reportedly begun paying gig workers for simple physical fixes. Vision-language models can now write the task description automatically.
revenue_model: 20-30% take on each task plus a monthly platform fee per fleet.
non_obvious_insight: Every robot fleet needs a thin, geographically spread hands-and-feet layer that scales with robot count. A two-sided micro-labor network is cheaper than dedicated field teams, and because the robot is the buyer, demand is programmable and grows with every deployment.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a delivery-robot or campus-robot operator, recruit 50 local gig workers, and dispatch manually by SMS. Sign a $2k a month pilot with a small fleet, run 500 tasks, and publish resolution-time data.

title: Price-Raise Autopilot for One-Person Service Firms
one_liner: Find the underpriced clients in a solo operator's own invoice history and execute personalized price increases, paid as a share of the uplift.
customer: Nonemployer and 1-5 person service businesses with 50-800 repeat clients: groomers, cleaners, landscapers, bookkeepers, tutors, therapists, detailers.
problem: Rising costs are the top financial challenge, yet most solo operators have not repriced in years because they fear churn. The industry sells lead generation, not repricing, even though a modest increase on the bottom 40% of clients often beats a 20% lift in leads.
solution: Connect Stripe, Square, QuickBooks, Jobber or booking-software history. For each client, compute the effective hourly rate after drive time, materials and discounts, and rank clients as safe-to-raise or protect. Draft one-to-one messages in the owner's voice, send by text or email, track churn and replies, and roll back individual clients if needed. The dashboard shows before-and-after profit per hour.
why_now: The Fed's 2026 survey shows 76% of international sourcers already passed costs to customers, so consumers now accept increases. Payment and booking APIs give clean multi-year history, and LLMs write natural personal notes at zero marginal cost.
revenue_model: 15-20% of first-year incremental revenue captured (no uplift, no fee), or a $49/month plan for owners who prefer flat pricing.
non_obvious_insight: The industry assumes the number-one problem, getting customers, is the one to fix. For a business of one, the fastest path to profit is charging existing customers correctly, and owners are too close to their clients to do it themselves. Outcome pricing also works because the owner sees the money.
first_30_days: Run a concierge version for 20 groomers, cleaners and landscapers found in local Facebook groups, using exports and spreadsheets. Measure revenue lift and churn below 3%. Publish two before-and-after case studies and use them to price the software.

title: Bone-First Strength Program for Women 45+
one_liner: A gym-delivered lifting and impact program for perimenopausal women, sold on DEXA-verified bone and muscle results.
customer: Women aged roughly 42-60 paying $79-149 per month, delivered through independent gyms, Pilates and strength studios and PT clinics that license the program.
problem: Women's fitness tech is fixated on cycle-syncing even though current evidence for cycle effects on performance is inconclusive, while midlife women (an 'invisible cohort' in sports science) face accelerating bone and muscle loss, worsened for those on GLP-1 drugs. Gyms sell toning and never measure the outcome that matters.
solution: A 24-week program of progressive heavy lifting, impact and balance work, with DEXA at baseline, 6 and 12 months via partner scan providers, simple bone-loading dose tracking with a hip or wrist sensor, coach training and a results dashboard studios use for retention. Positioned as wellness and performance with a physician advisor, not treatment.
why_now: Retail DEXA scans have dropped to roughly sub-$100, menopause is a mainstream topic, wearable makers are pouring money into women's health, perimenopause research is accelerating in 2026, and GLP-1 adoption has made bone and lean-mass loss a mass-market worry.
revenue_model: Member fees $79-149 per month; studio license $299-499 per month plus $30 per member; scan affiliate margin of $10-20 per scan.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is the outcome measurement: 'X percent of members held or gained bone density at 12 months' is a claim no gym can currently make, and the resulting dataset is valuable to clinicians and researchers. Cycle-syncing is a distraction from the larger midlife need.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 women aged 45-60 through two local strength gyms, book baseline DEXA scans with a retail or mobile provider, run a 12-week pilot with a physician advisor, and sign three studios to license the program off the interim results.

title: Swarf Stabilization for New US Magnet Plants
one_liner: Hazmat-grade stabilization, transport and recycler routing for the pyrophoric NdFeB grinding swarf that new US magnet plants will produce in tonnes.
customer: New and expanding US sintered-magnet makers and independent magnet grinding shops, who pay per-kg handling. Recyclers and re-melters are the downstream buyers.
problem: US magnet capacity is ramping (MP Materials broke ground on a Texas magnet campus in Feb 2026 on a DoD-backed deal). Machining and grinding turn a large share of sintered NdFeB, often 20-30%, into oil-wet, self-heating swarf and sludge. It is hard to classify, ship and store, so it drifts to overseas buyers or hazardous-waste disposal.
solution: An inerting and oil-immersion protocol, DOT-compliant packaging for self-heating solids, permitted storage through a partner, and routing to domestic recyclers or re-melters. It comes with a mass-balance certificate that lets the magnet maker claim recycled content to defense and EU customers.
why_now: Trace the chain: DoD equity and DPA-style support create new US magnet plants, which create swarf, which becomes a fire and compliance problem with no dedicated service. EU rare-earth recycled-content obligations phase in 2028-2032, and recyclers such as Cyclic Materials are funded and hunting for clean feed.
revenue_model: Handling fee per kg, plus a revenue share of recovered oxide or alloy value from recyclers, plus an annual compliance retainer.
non_obvious_insight: The near-term rare-earth urban mine is inside the factory. Swarf is clean, known-composition and available in tonnes before any end-of-life magnet wave arrives.
first_30_days: Call EHS heads at the 5 new or ramping magnet plants and 10 grinding shops. Offer a free swarf audit to quantify tonnage and value. Line up a hazmat-permitted storage and transport partner and one recycler offtake. Run a first pilot shipment.

title: Telemetry-Underwritten Credit for Defense Sub-Tier Shops
one_liner: Plug low-cost MTConnect adapters into shop CNC machines to create tamper-evident proof of utilization and surge capacity that unlocks equipment loans and rated-order credit lines, and gives primes the capacity data they lack.
customer: 10-50 person machine shops, foundries and sheet-metal shops pursuing defense work (they pay $149-299 a month). Lenders, CDFIs and equipment lessors pay origination fees, and primes and state defense-industrial-base offices later pay for verified-capacity queries.
problem: An industry study finds 'no fit-for-purpose investment model' between R&D and mature production for sub-tier suppliers (castings, forgings, sensors, rocket motors), with VC a sliver and PE putting in only $1-3B a year. Hadrian raised $1.37B while metals robot orders rose just 3% in H1, and shops cannot fund a machine or a cobot cell. Lenders underwrite job shops on tax returns and collateral, and DoD has no real-time data on free spindle-hours.
solution: A hardware-light MTConnect and OPC UA adapter kit and cloud service that logs spindle utilization, part counts, scrap and on-time delivery with signed, tamper-evident records. It issues a 'verified capacity score', lender-ready utilization letters and attestations for DPAS-rated orders, and an anonymized open-capacity feed for primes and government. Partner lenders extend equipment loans and rated-order lines against the score.
why_now: Rated orders, drone and munitions surges and Navy co-investment are pushing demand to sub-tiers just as the Navy stops funding early stages. Publicly funded defense-industrial-base lending vehicles need originators. Modern CNC controls already speak MTConnect, so the marginal hardware cost is small.
revenue_model: $149-299 a month per shop for telemetry and score, 1-2% origination fee from lenders on funded loans, and later a per-query fee from primes and agencies for verified surge capacity.
non_obvious_insight: Utilization telemetry is a better credit signal than a tax return for a job shop, and it doubles as the surge-capacity data the government has never had. The same tamper-evident record serves the lender, the prime and the auditor, so shops pay because it gets them financed.
first_30_days: Partner with a manufacturing extension center and one CDFI or equipment lessor. Install adapters on 10 machines in a defense-heavy cluster (Connecticut or Ohio) and produce the first 3 verified utilization letters to test whether a lender will price better against them.

title: Vetted Remote Operators for Home Robots
one_liner: A privacy-audited, background-checked, insured pool of remote operators who take over home and warehouse robots at their hard moments, sold to robot makers as the trust layer for teleoperation.
customer: Home-robot, service-robot and warehouse-robot makers pay $18-35 per operator-hour. Operators are displaced support and ops workers earning $22-30 an hour.
problem: The first consumer humanoids (such as 1X's NEO) ship in 2026 relying on remote humans who can see inside homes, which raised a privacy backlash. Robot startups lack a scalable, vetted, insured operator workforce and would otherwise use anonymous offshore BPOs, while buyers want accountable domestic operators.
solution: Recruit and train from displaced call-centre, ops and gaming talent. A standard teleop certification, privacy protocols (blurred or avatarised feeds, no recording, no-go zones), session audit logs, background checks and E&O/cyber insurance form the service. Scheduling covers time zones and performance metrics track intervention success. Start with warehouse or delivery robots, then homes.
why_now: Consumer humanoid preorders and shipments began in 2025-26 with teleop as the fallback, warehouse and sidewalk robots are at scale, and privacy concerns make trust a differentiator.
revenue_model: 30-40% margin per operator-hour, certification fees and an insurance premium share.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for robots is not hardware but trusted remote labor, and every teleop intervention also trains the policy. Privacy trust, not price, is the moat, and it reframes displaced workers as a new 'robot pilot' class.
first_30_days: Contact 20 robotics startups (delivery, warehouse, cleaning) with a pilot of 5 vetted operators for 200 hours at cost. Write the privacy protocol and audit template. Recruit 30 candidates from laid-off support and ops staff.

title: Certified Coder Audit Pods for Autonomous Coding
one_liner: Displaced medical coders, organised as credentialed audit pods, provide the sampled human sign-off that lets hospitals trust autonomous coding AI to submit claims.
customer: Autonomous medical-coding vendors who need a human audit layer to close hospital deals, hospital revenue-cycle compliance leaders and physician groups. Pricing is $1.5-4 per audited chart or $15-40k a month per pod.
problem: Coding is a highly exposed white-collar job, and coders are being cut as autonomous coding reaches production. But billing compliance (False Claims Act exposure, payer and RAC audits) needs accountable, credentialed review. Vendors' own audit teams are thin or offshore and unlicensed.
solution: Pods of 5-10 CPC/CCS-certified ex-coders with a lead auditor, receiving risk-stratified samples of AI-coded charts via API. They provide error-taxonomy dashboards, monthly compliance attestations, feedback loops that retrain the model and contractual accuracy thresholds.
why_now: Autonomous coding moved into production in 2025-26, the coder job pool is shrinking, payers are using AI audits themselves and hospital margins are under pressure.
revenue_model: Per-chart fees or pod retainers at 45-55% gross margin, plus premium attestation packages.
non_obvious_insight: Full automation in healthcare billing stalls at the accountability signature, and the people displaced are the ones who can provide it. The human role shifts from doing to auditing a 5-10% sample, which is recurring compliance spend rather than labor cost. The audit data is also valuable training data for the vendor.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 laid-off certified coders through AAPC and AHIMA forums. Pitch 5 autonomous-coding startups a pilot: audit 1,000 charts at about $2 each with a written accuracy report. Sign one as a design partner.

title: Contingency-Fee 45F Childcare Tax Credit Shop
one_liner: An R&D-credit-style boutique that finds, structures and files the newly expanded employer childcare credit (40%, or 50% for small businesses, capped at $500k/$600k) for firms already spending on childcare.
customer: Mid-market employers (200-5,000 staff) with onsite care or vendor childcare spend: hospitals, manufacturers, universities, credit unions and restaurant chains. Referral channel: their CPA firms.
problem: The 45F credit was rarely used under its old cap. From January 1, 2026 the credit rose to 40% (50% small business) with $500k ($600k) caps. Eligibility turns on contract structure, licensing, enrollment open to employees and documentation, and it interacts with the new $7,500 DCFSA limit. Generalist CPAs don't know it and CFOs have never claimed it.
solution: A two-week diagnostic reviews contracts and spend, restructures where needed (for example, reserved-slot agreements with licensed local centers or consortium models), computes the credit and files the forms alongside the client's CPA. Reserved-slot deals also give centers guaranteed enrollment, which helps supply.
why_now: The changes took effect January 2026, employers set 2027 benefit budgets in Q4 2026, and the first full filing season under the new rules is early 2027.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 15-20% of credit claimed (a $250k credit yields $40-50k). Add-on brokerage fee for slot-reservation contracts.
non_obvious_insight: A $500k cap means the credit can fund a whole classroom's worth of care per employer. The constraint is know-how, not money, and reserved-slot contracts turn a tax credit into childcare supply, a desert fix hidden in the tax code.
first_30_days: Partner with a tax attorney or CPA who has done R&D or WOTC credits. Build a list of 200 employers advertising childcare benefits (job posts, hospital filings). Publish a two-page 45F guide and a free eligibility screen. Aim for 3 signed contingency engagements.

title: Cloud-Bricking Escrow for Hardware Brands
one_liner: A neutral escrow-and-standby service that holds a hardware brand's cloud backend and local-mode firmware, and takes over the moment the cloud vendor fails.
customer: Consumer-hardware brands that outsource their cloud or app to an ODM or startup: private-label and licensed smart-home, router, EV-charger, pet-tech and e-bike brands. Retailers and insurers are secondary buyers.
problem: When a small backend vendor dies, the brand that sold the device takes the blame. Motorola-branded routers stopped being manageable when the MotoSync+ app failed. Play Store reviews say a third-party backend host's licence expired and the host ended operations ('Server Licence Expired'). Users report months without a fix. Spotify Car Thing became 'a $200 hardware turned into e-waste overnight.' An HN commenter estimated $300k-600k to open-source a single project, so afterthought rescue is unaffordable.
solution: For a flat annual fee, the brand deposits its backend container images and infrastructure-as-code, sealed secrets, signed 'local mode' firmware or companion-app builds, and device protocol docs. The operator monitors cloud health, domain and cert expiry, app-store status and vendor solvency signals. On a trigger it either runs the backend on standby infrastructure (pay-per-device) or releases the local-mode build. Brands that certify get an 'Afterlife Ready' mark for retail listings and regulator conversations.
why_now: EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations began on 11 Sept 2026, with full manufacturer obligations from 11 Dec 2027 and lifecycle handling required. Startup shutdowns are running at a high rate: 14.4% of H1 2026 shutdowns were AI companies with a median age of 2.3 years and a median $30k cash at closure. Recent bricking cases (Motorola routers in Jun 2026, Nest thermostats, Kodak Pulse frames, Samsung fridges in Sept 2026) are fresh in retailers' minds.
revenue_model: $5-25k/yr escrow subscription per brand, plus $0.10-0.50/device/month for hot standby and a per-incident recovery fee. Certification audits are a later add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The liability chain runs from a dead vendor through the brand to the customer, and existing escrow (software licence escrow, to my knowledge) is not built for live device fleets. Evidence: the Motorola router thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48425611, 238 points) traces the outage to a third-party server licence expiring after the host company ended operations. The 'when hardware goes EOL' essay (https://www.marcia.no/words/eol; HN discussion at https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46609492, 403 points) lists Nest, Car Thing and Kodak Pulse. It quotes the $300k-600k open-sourcing estimate and community workarounds (OpenWRT, 'No Longer Evil'). The EU CRA page (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act) sets the 11 Sept 2026 and 11 Dec 2027 dates. The buyer is the brand, not the consumer, and the fee has to be cheaper than a single recall.
first_30_days: Week 1: build a free 'BackendWatch' monitor that pings a brand's cloud endpoints, cert expiry and domain renewals. Week 2: cold-email 50 licensed-brand and private-label hardware companies, and Kickstarter-scale hardware founders. Weeks 3-4: sign 3 design partners on a $2.5k pilot escrow. Write the trigger contract with a startup-insolvency lawyer.

title: Twelve-Week Friend Pods, Paid by Cafes
one_liner: Fixed cohorts of six adults meet weekly at the same cafe for 12 weeks, backed by a refundable attendance deposit, with the venue paying for guaranteed slow-hour covers.
customer: Two payers. Adults 25-45 who moved cities or lost their friend group ($75 refundable deposit plus about $25 a month). Independent cafes, bars and climbing gyms paying roughly $8-12 per seat-night for guaranteed off-peak traffic.
problem: Friend-making products optimize the first meeting, and one-off stranger dinners rarely convert. Research on friendship formation (Hall, 2018) puts casual friendship at roughly 50 hours together and real friendship at about 90. Meanwhile 24% of US adults with only a high-school education report zero close friends (up from 3% in 1990). Every app's economics reward churn, not durable friendship.
solution: Pods of 6 matched by neighborhood and schedule, not personality. 12 weekly 2.5-hour sessions at one partner venue, with a trained host for the first four weeks who then fades out. The deposit is refunded per session attended. After week 12 the pod 'graduates' into a standing-table subscription. Hosts earn a bonus tied to the share of pod members still meeting at week 20.
why_now: Bumble cut 30% of staff (Jun 2025) and relaunched BFF around groups (Sep 2025), which shows demand for friend-making but not retention. Run clubs proved people pay for recurring in-person belonging. Independent venues face weak weekday traffic and want guaranteed covers.
revenue_model: Membership of about $25 a month per member, forfeited deposits (typically 10-15%), and a per-seat-night fee from venues. Host bonuses are the main cost. Scales city by city with a lean local ops lead.
non_obvious_insight: Friendship is a dose problem, not a matching problem. Every product is paid at the moment of the first meeting, so all of them optimize matches. The only metric worth charging on is hours-together at week 20. Venues, not users, are the natural payer for attendance, because a seated pod is guaranteed revenue on a dead Tuesday.
first_30_days: Pick one neighborhood. Sign 6 cafes with dead Tuesday-Thursday slots on a flat per-seat guarantee. Recruit 4 pods (24 people) through local run-club and Instagram audiences and collect the $75 deposits up front (about $1,800 of first cash). Hire 2 part-time hosts and start week 1 in month 2. Track attendance at weeks 6 and 12.

title: Made-in-USA Proof Files for Relabeling Brands
one_liner: Audit-ready substantiation files and monitoring for brands rushing to claim 'Made in USA' after tariffs.
customer: Consumer and industrial brands with $5M-$300M revenue and retailer private-label teams, buying through general counsel or the ecommerce head.
problem: Tariffs make US-made claims valuable, but an unqualified 'Made in USA' claim needs 'all or virtually all' US content and processing under FTC rules, with civil penalties per violation and state-law class actions on top. Brands switch suppliers on cost and forget the claim. Suppliers cannot document origin per component.
solution: Software plus service that maps each SKU's BOM to component and labor origin, gathers supplier attestations and mill certs, scores the claim, drafts compliant packaging and listing language ('Assembled in USA with global parts', or percent US), monitors marketplace listings and supplier changes, and builds a defense binder.
why_now: A reshoring marketing wave, supplier switching under tariffs, and active enforcement risk. The same BOM data that supports tariff compliance supports the claim.
revenue_model: $3-15k per product-line audit plus $500-2k a month for monitoring. Retailer programs that require proof.
non_obvious_insight: The first legal casualty of the reshoring wave is the label. Brands that reshore partially and market fully carry hidden liability, and a file built once serves both marketing and customs defense. The buyer is legal or marketing, not customs, so this avoids the crowded tariff-software budget.
first_30_days: Scan Amazon 'Made in USA' listings for weak claims using public data. Send a three-page claim risk scorecard to the brands. Sell the first 10 audits at $3k with a partner advertising lawyer signing off.
